common_name: Blue Coco Pole Bean (French Heirloom Snap, Shell, and Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow at the base of a sturdy pole or trellis once soil has warmed after last frost; pick young for snap use, or leave pods to mature for fresh shelling or dry storage beans.

directions: Blue Coco is a dual- to triple-purpose French heirloom pole bean bearing slender, bluish-purple pods on vines with purple-tinged leaves and lavender flowers, an attractive plant as much at home on an ornamental trellis as in the vegetable rows. Young pods snap tender with a mild, sweet flavor, while pods left to fill out yield plump beans with rich chocolate-brown seed coats that shell fresh or dry down for winter soup beans. Its origins are debated, with some tracing the name to Central America rather than France, but it has circulated in French seed trade and heirloom collections for generations. Provide a tall, sturdy support, since the vigorous vines climb readily and produce over a long season when picked regularly.

common_name: Blauhilde Pole Bean (Deep Purple German Heirloom Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed to at least 60F; provide a tall trellis or pole tepee, since vines climb to about 9 feet and crop continuously through the season.

directions: Blauhilde is a German heirloom pole bean prized for its striking deep purple pods, which grow long and wide yet stay tender and stringless, set off nicely against rose-purple blossoms. The pods turn green when cooked but hold their purple color when lightly steamed, making raw and blanched harvests fun to tell apart in the kitchen. Vigorous, disease-tolerant vines bear over a long window when picked at 6-8 inches, and the plant's dramatic coloring makes it a popular choice for growers who want both a productive snap bean and an ornamental accent on the trellis.

common_name: Kwintus Pole Bean (Early Riser Dutch Flat-Podded Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis; Kwintus matures roughly two weeks earlier than standard pole beans like Kentucky Wonder, making it a good choice for shorter seasons.

directions: Kwintus, also sold as Early Riser, is a Dutch-bred flat-podded pole bean that combines the buttery texture of an Italian Romano type with unusually early maturity for a climbing bean. Pods grow 8-10 inches long, broad and stringless, and stay tender and flavorful even as they size up on the vine, which makes for a more forgiving harvest window than narrow round-podded snap beans. Vigorous 6-9 foot vines need sturdy support and reward regular picking with continuous production through the season. Its combination of early cropping and long harvest tolerance has made it a favorite among market gardeners and home growers alike.

common_name: Meraviglia di Venezia Pole Bean (Marvel of Venice Yellow Romano Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost and provide a trellis or poles at least 7 feet tall; pick frequently to keep this prolific climber producing.

directions: Meraviglia di Venezia, known in English as Marvel of Venice, is an Italian heirloom pole bean bearing flat, lemon-yellow Romano-type pods up to 10 inches long with a buttery texture and no stringiness. It is an early-maturing, white-seeded strain of this classic Venetian bean, ready to pick in about 55 days, notably fast for a climbing variety. The meaty pods hold their quality well even as they lengthen on the vine and are traditionally sliced and dressed simply with lemon, olive oil, and herbs. Because it has become uncommon in commercial production, it is listed on the Slow Food Foundation's Ark of Taste as a variety worth preserving.
sources: Slow Food Foundation Ark of Taste

common_name: Kentucky Wonder Wax Pole Bean (Yellow-Podded Heirloom Pole Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; a yellow-podded sport of standard Kentucky Wonder, it needs the same tall support and regular picking.

directions: Kentucky Wonder Wax is a yellow-podded selection of the classic brown-seeded Kentucky Wonder pole bean, offering the same vigorous climbing habit and heavy yields but with round, buttery-yellow pods instead of green. Pods run 7-8 inches, stringless and meaty, with a slightly sweeter, more delicate flavor than the green original, and they show up clearly against the foliage for easy picking. Like its parent variety, it climbs readily to 6-8 feet and needs a sturdy trellis, rewarding gardeners with continuous production when harvested every few days. It remains a favorite where gardeners want a wax bean with genuine pole-bean vigor rather than a compact bush habit.

common_name: Selma Zesta Pole Bean (Zelma Zesta Heirloom Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; a lesser-known heirloom kept in circulation mainly through regional seed savers and small seed houses.

directions: Selma Zesta, also circulated under the spelling Zelma Zesta, is a Southern heirloom pole snap bean maintained in small-scale seed exchange circles rather than mass commercial production. Vigorous climbing vines produce rounded, fleshy pods with good snap-bean flavor and texture, harvested young for fresh eating in the tradition of Appalachian and Southern cornfield-style pole beans. It is a good candidate for gardeners looking to grow out and help preserve a regionally distinct heirloom that has not been widely commercialized. Provide a tall, sturdy support and pick regularly to keep vines productive through the season.

common_name: Selma Zebra Pole Bean (Purple-Streaked Early Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost at the base of a trellis or pole; matures earlier than many pole beans, making it useful where the growing season is shorter.

directions: Selma Zebra is a distinctively marked pole snap bean, its green pods streaked with purple zigzag patterning that fades somewhat when cooked but makes for an eye-catching harvest basket. It matures notably early for a climbing bean, and the tender, fleshy pods are best picked young for fresh snap use. Like other regionally maintained heirlooms, it is kept alive mainly through small seed companies and seed-saver networks rather than large commercial catalogs. Give it a sturdy trellis and pick often to encourage continued pod set through the growing season.

common_name: Landreth Stringless Bush Bean (1885 American Heirloom Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost danger has passed; no support needed for this compact bush variety, and successive sowings extend the harvest.

directions: Landreth Stringless is an American heirloom bush bean first offered by the D. Landreth Seed Company in the 1880s and notable historically as one of the earliest widely marketed stringless snap beans, a trait that was a genuine novelty in that era. It produces medium-green pods a little over 5 inches long with a meaty texture and good flavor, backed by seeds in a rich chocolate-brown color. The plant matures quickly and yields heavily over a relatively short window, making it a reliable choice for succession planting and home canning. Its long, continuous availability from Landreth makes it one of the oldest still-commercially-offered American bean varieties.

common_name: Enorma Runner Bean (British Exhibition Scarlet Runner)

planting.note: Sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis or obelisk around last frost; runner beans prefer cool summer nights and drop flowers in intense heat.

directions: Enorma is a long-established British exhibition runner bean, holder of the RHS Award of Garden Merit, prized by show growers for its extremely long, smooth, slender pods that can reach 20 inches under good conditions. Bright scarlet flowers cover the vigorous vines early and heavily, drawing hummingbirds and bumblebees and setting an abundant crop over a long season. Pods are best picked well before they reach exhibition length for eating quality, since very long pods used for showing tend to be tougher and more fibrous. Give it a tall, sturdy support, since well-fed plants can climb well over 8 feet.

common_name: Celebration Runner Bean (Salmon-Pink Flowered Ornamental-Edible Runner)

planting.note: Sow at the base of a tall trellis, arch, or obelisk around last frost; the soft pink flowers make it as suited to a flower border as to the vegetable garden.

directions: Celebration is a British-bred runner bean, an RHS Award of Garden Merit winner grown as much for its fragrant, salmon-pink flowers as for its harvest. The blossoms are a gentler color than the typical scarlet runner bean bloom, making the plant a popular dual-purpose choice for gardeners who want an ornamental flowering vine that also produces a real crop of pods. Long, smooth, nearly stringless pods form heavily and stay tender when picked young, and the variety shows good tolerance to rust compared with older runner bean types. Its early cropping habit and rust tolerance have made it a reliable choice in cooler, damper climates where runner beans are a garden staple.

common_name: Black Coat Runner Bean (1600s Heirloom Black-Seeded Runner)

planting.note: Sow at the base of a tall, sturdy trellis around last frost; grown as much for its flowers and dry seed as for snap use.

directions: Black Coat is among the oldest documented runner beans still in cultivation, with references to it in European botanical writing dating back to the 1600s, long before most modern runner bean cultivars existed. Its flowers range from deep orange to cherry-red and are heavily visited by hummingbirds, while young pods can be picked for snap use in the same way as other runner beans. Left to mature, the pods yield glossy black seeds that dry well for winter storage and cooking, giving the variety a genuine dual purpose. Because of its age and rarity, it is grown today mostly by heirloom seed savers and gardeners interested in historic bean varieties.

common_name: Chicago Warted Hubbard Squash (1894 Heirloom Winter Storage Squash)

planting.note: Direct-sow in hills after soil has warmed to at least 70F and frost danger has passed; give the sprawling vines ample room.

directions: Chicago Warted Hubbard is an 1894 heirloom winter squash introduced by a Chicago seed house and it remains one of the more heavily warted, thick-shelled Hubbard-type squashes still grown today. The dusky olive-green, deeply wrinkled rind protects finely textured, sweet orange flesh that keeps exceptionally well in a cool, dry location, often lasting well into spring. Its dense flesh and excellent storage life made it a favorite for canning and pies in the era before mechanical refrigeration was common. The vigorous vines need significant space and a long, warm season to fully size and cure their large fruit.

common_name: Green Hubbard Squash (True Green Improved Hubbard)

planting.note: Direct-sow in hills after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; needs a long, warm season and plenty of room to vine.

directions: Green Hubbard, sometimes offered as True Green Improved Hubbard, is regarded by many seed historians as the original Hubbard type from which the more familiar blue- and orange-skinned Hubbard squashes were later selected. It bears large, teardrop-shaped fruit with a hard, dark green rind that is smoother and less warted than the later Chicago Warted strain, protecting dense, dry, golden-orange flesh with a rich, sweet flavor well suited to soups and purees. Like other Hubbard types, well-cured fruit stores for months in a cool, dry spot, making it a genuine long-season keeper squash. It needs generous vine space and a full warm season to size up and fully mature before harvest.

common_name: Small Wonder Spaghetti Squash (Compact Personal-Size Hybrid)

planting.note: Direct-sow or transplant after frost danger has passed; the compact vine takes noticeably less space than standard spaghetti squash.

directions: Small Wonder is a hybrid spaghetti squash bred for a compact, space-saving vine that still delivers high yields of personal-sized fruit, each weighing roughly 1.5 to 2 pounds, about half the size of standard spaghetti squash. The oval fruit yield the same pale-yellow, stringy flesh that separates into spaghetti-like strands when cooked, making it well suited to single servings without the leftovers a full-sized fruit produces. Because the vines take up notably less garden space than traditional spaghetti squash, it is a practical choice for smaller vegetable beds or intensive plantings. It also matures somewhat earlier than many full-sized spaghetti squash varieties, giving a head start in shorter growing seasons.
